I've farmed this land for fifty years. My father farmed it before me. I know this soil — it holds water decently from the well, and the wheat-maize rotation has always served me well. My grandchildren are in the city now, my son drives trucks part of the year, so I handle most of the fieldwork myself with some hired machinery for planting and harvest. I can't afford to experiment much at my age. I do what works.

For wheat, I plant in early October once the maize comes off. I'll use 济麦22 — I've grown it for years, it's reliable in our county, tolerates drought reasonably well. I'll rotary-till before planting. I put down base fertilizer — compound fertilizer plus urea — before seeding, then top-dress with urea in spring around jointing. Three irrigations: the winter water before freeze, the jointing water, and one at grain-filling. I spray herbicide in winter and a fungicide pass in late spring for rust. I expect around 450 jin per mu if the season is normal.

For maize, I plant straight after wheat harvest in June — no-till, machine-planted. Hybrid seed, 郑单958 or whatever the seed shop has that year in that family. Summer gets more rain so I only irrigate if there's a dry stretch in August. I apply base fertilizer at planting and chase it with urea when the plant is knee-high. One herbicide spray early, one pest pass if I see worms. Yield around 550 jin per mu.

I split the land roughly half and half. No big changes this year. My back isn't what it was.
